conditions.quote: have not been able to drill for three days

healthContext: Henry describes a genuine illness that kept him off drill for three days and required the surgeon's medicine — unnamed, but consistent with the febrile complaints endemic to camps on damp ground. He shrewdly blames sleeping on the ground and the locale's 'fever and ague' (malaria), framing the ague as a danger to be avoided rather than a present diagnosis.

conditions.quote: I have had the rheumatism very bad, am over it now

healthContext: Henry recounts a severe, mobility-disabling bout of rheumatism ('I had it so bad before that, I could hardly walk') that he attributes to sleeping on bare ground, with a 95-cent wooden tent floor serving as both remedy and prophylaxis. Though he reports full recovery and softens the news with humor, the episode marks the musculoskeletal toll of cold, damp autumn camp life.

Alexander affirms he is 'safe and sound' and well after a grueling nine-day, 500-mile movement to the front. He notes the regiment 'all suffered from hunger' at Kalorama Heights — dubbed 'Starvation Heights' — a transient commissary-failure deprivation now past, compounded by sleeping on cold ground; his pronounced loneliness is emotional strain, not physical illness.

Henry reports no ailment. He emphasizes conditions protective against winter sickness — ample rations 'of the right sort' and heavy new blankets keeping the men warm through freezing nights; the death he relays (Albert Savage) is a home/civilian loss, not a camp casualty.
